title: Evolution of human bipedalism
summary: Walking upright developed gradually. Between 7 and 6 million years ago Sahelanthropus may have walked on two legs, and the oldest evidence for it comes from fossils of the earliest known humans. For millions of years these walkers kept features that helped them climb trees. By 1.8 million years ago, our ancestors had long legs and an efficient striding gait suited to travelling longer distances.

uncertainty.note: Chronology spans the earliest proposed bipedal fossil indicators around 7–6 Ma to the consolidation of modern striding bipedalism by roughly 1.8 Ma.

where.modern_name: Toros-Menalla locality TM 266, Djurab Desert, northern Chad (reference site for Sahelanthropus; bipedalism evolved across central and eastern Africa)
where.historical_name: Chadian lake-margin and African woodland-savanna mosaic; no human polities existed

importance.justification: The primary anatomical innovation distinguishing the hominin clade from other apes, fundamentally restructuring the skeleton and freeing the forelimbs for tool manufacture.

related.because: Freeing the forelimbs through habitual upright posture was a physical prerequisite for grasping hammerstones and striking flaked stone tools.
